notes:
Basic terms

  • System: part of universe under study; surroundings: rest. Types: open (exchanges matter & energy), closed (only energy), isolated (neither).
  • State functions (depend only on initial/final state): $U$, $H$, $S$, $G$, $P$, $V$, $T$. Path functions: heat $q$, work $w$.
  • Sign convention (IUPAC): heat absorbed by system $+q$; work done ON system $+w$.

First law

  • $\Delta U = q + w$ (energy conservation). For expansion against constant external pressure: $w = -p_{ext}\Delta V$. Isothermal reversible (ideal gas): $w = -nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$.
  • Enthalpy: $H = U + pV$; at constant pressure $\Delta H = \Delta U + p\Delta V = q_p$. $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$ for reactions involving gases.
  • $C_p - C_v = R$ (per mole, ideal gas). $C_p/C_v = \gamma$.

Thermochemistry

Enthalpy typeMeaning
$\Delta_f H^\circ$Formation of 1 mol compound from elements in standard states; $\Delta_fH^\circ$ of an element = 0
$\Delta_c H^\circ$Complete combustion of 1 mol substance in O$_2$ (always negative)
$\Delta_{sol}H, \Delta_{fus}H, \Delta_{vap}H$Solution, fusion (melting), vaporisation

Hess's law: $\Delta H$ for a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or several, since $H$ is a state function — allows adding/subtracting thermochemical equations to get $\Delta H$ of a target reaction.

Second law & entropy

  • Entropy $S$ is a measure of disorder/randomness; $\Delta S_{universe} > 0$ for a spontaneous process (2nd law). $\Delta S = q_{rev}/T$.
  • $\Delta S > 0$: solid → liquid → gas, dissolution, increase in moles of gas.

Gibbs energy & spontaneity

  • $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ (at constant $T,P$). $\Delta G < 0$: spontaneous; $\Delta G = 0$: equilibrium; $\Delta G > 0$: non-spontaneous (needs external work).
  • $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -2.303RT\log K$.
$\Delta H$$\Delta S$Spontaneity
$-$$+$always spontaneous
$+$$-$never spontaneous
$-$$-$spontaneous at low $T$
$+$$+$spontaneous at high $T$

Third law

The entropy of a perfectly crystalline substance is zero at 0 K, allowing absolute entropy values to be calculated.

Exam tip

2 questions typically: a Hess's-law numerical (add/subtract given $\Delta H$ values), and a $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ spontaneity/sign-based question. Watch sign conventions on work done.

questions.q: For an isolated system, which of the following is correct?
options: Both matter and energy can be exchanged freely
Neither matter nor energy can be exchanged with surroundings
questions.explanation: An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings (e.g. an ideal thermos flask).

questions.q: According to the IUPAC sign convention, if a gas absorbs 200 J of heat and does 50 J of work on the surroundings, $\Delta U$ is
questions.explanation: $q = +200$ J (absorbed); $w = -50$ J (done by system). $\Delta U = q + w = 200 - 50 = 150$ J.

questions.q: Which of the following is a state function?
questions.explanation: Enthalpy $H$ depends only on the initial and final states, unlike heat and work, which depend on the path taken.

questions.q: For the reaction $N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \to 2NH_3(g)$, the relation between $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$ is
questions.explanation: $\Delta n_g = 2 - (1+3) = -2$. $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT = \Delta U - 2RT$.

questions.q: One mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly from 10 L to 20 L at 300 K. The work done (w, IUPAC convention) is ($R = 8.314\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $w = -nRT\ln(V_2/V_1) = -1\times8.314\times300\times\ln2 = -8.314\times300\times0.693 \approx -1729$ J.

questions.q: Hess's law is a direct consequence of the fact that
questions.explanation: Since $H$ depends only on initial and final states, the total $\Delta H$ for a reaction is the same regardless of the number of steps taken.

questions.q: Given: $C(s) + O_2(g) \to CO_2(g)$, $\Delta H = -393.5\,\text{kJ}$ and $CO(g) + \tfrac12O_2(g) \to CO_2(g)$, $\Delta H = -283.0\,\text{kJ}$. The enthalpy of formation of CO(g) is
questions.explanation: $\Delta H_f(CO) = \Delta H_1 - \Delta H_2 = -393.5 - (-283.0) = -110.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ (subtracting the second equation from the first).

questions.q: For a spontaneous process, the second law of thermodynamics requires that
questions.explanation: A spontaneous process increases the total entropy of the universe (system + surroundings), even if the system's own entropy decreases.

questions.q: For which of the following processes is $\Delta S$ negative?
questions.explanation: Moles of gas decrease from 4 to 2, decreasing randomness, so $\Delta S < 0$. The other processes increase disorder.

questions.q: A reaction has $\Delta H = -50\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta S = -100\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$. It is spontaneous
questions.explanation: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$; with $\Delta H<0$ and $\Delta S<0$, $\Delta G$ stays negative only while $T$ is small enough that $T\Delta S$ doesn't outweigh $\Delta H$: spontaneous at low $T$.

questions.q: The standard Gibbs energy change is related to the equilibrium constant by
questions.explanation: $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -2.303RT\log K$; a large $K$ (product-favoured) gives a large negative $\Delta G^\circ$.

questions.q: According to the third law of thermodynamics, the entropy of a perfectly crystalline substance at 0 K is
questions.explanation: At 0 K a perfect crystal has only one possible microstate (perfect order), so its entropy is taken as zero.

questions.q: For an ideal gas, $C_p - C_v$ equals
questions.explanation: From $H = U + pV = U + RT$ (per mole ideal gas), differentiating w.r.t. $T$ gives $C_p - C_v = R$.

questions.q: Combustion reactions are always
questions.explanation: Combustion in oxygen releases energy as heat and light, so $\Delta_cH$ is always negative (exothermic).

questions.q: Work done on the system during a free expansion of an ideal gas into vacuum ($p_{ext}=0$) is
questions.explanation: $w = -p_{ext}\Delta V$; since $p_{ext} = 0$ (vacuum), no work is done, whatever the volume change.

questions.q: If $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$ for a reaction, it will be spontaneous
questions.explanation: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ becomes negative only when $T$ is large enough that $T\Delta S$ exceeds $\Delta H$: spontaneous at high $T$.

questions.q: The enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is taken as
options: equal to its enthalpy of combustion
questions.explanation: By convention, the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its most stable form is zero (reference point).

questions.q: A process for which $q = 0$ is called
questions.explanation: In an adiabatic process no heat is exchanged with the surroundings ($q=0$), so $\Delta U = w$.

questions.q: 2 mol of an ideal gas at constant pressure of 1 atm expands from 5 L to 10 L. The work done (w, IUPAC convention) is (1 L atm = 101.3 J)
questions.explanation: $w = -p\Delta V = -1\times(10-5) = -5$ L atm $= -5\times101.3 = -506.5$ J (work done on the system is negative since the gas expands against external pressure).

questions.q: Which of the following has the largest (most positive) entropy?
questions.explanation: Gases have the highest degree of molecular disorder/randomness compared to liquids and solids, hence the highest entropy.

questions.q: Which of the following is an intensive property?
questions.explanation: Intensive properties (temperature, pressure, density) do not depend on the amount of substance, unlike extensive properties (volume, mass, heat capacity).

questions.q: 100 g of water is heated from 25 °C to 35 °C. The heat absorbed is (specific heat of water = 4.18 J g$^{-1}$ °C$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $q = mc\Delta T = 100\times4.18\times10 = 4180$ J $= 4.18$ kJ.

questions.q: The enthalpy of neutralisation of a strong acid with a strong base is
options: about $-57.3$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, nearly the same for all strong acid–strong base pairs
questions.explanation: Since strong acids and bases are fully ionised, neutralisation is essentially $H^+ + OH^- \to H_2O$ in every case, releasing about 57.3 kJ per mole of water formed.

questions.q: Using bond enthalpies H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242, H–Cl = 431 kJ mol$^{-1}$, the enthalpy change for $H_2(g) + Cl_2(g) \to 2HCl(g)$ is
questions.explanation: $\Delta H = \Sigma BE_{reactants} - \Sigma BE_{products} = (436+242) - 2(431) = 678 - 862 = -184$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

questions.q: The entropy change when 1 mol of ice melts at 273 K is (given $\Delta_{fus}H = 6.01$ kJ mol$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $\Delta S = \Delta H/T = 6010/273 \approx 22.0$ J K$^{-1}$mol$^{-1}$ (phase change occurs at constant $T$, so $q_{rev} = \Delta H$).

questions.q: Which of the following is an endothermic process?
questions.explanation: Melting requires energy input to break the lattice of hydrogen bonds in ice, so heat is absorbed ($\Delta H > 0$).

questions.q: For a process occurring at constant volume,
options: $q_v = \Delta U$, since no p-V work is done at constant volume
questions.explanation: At constant volume, $\Delta V = 0$ so $w = -p\Delta V = 0$, and from the first law $\Delta U = q_v + w = q_v$.

questions.q: The enthalpy of atomisation of a substance is
options: the energy released when a compound forms from its elements
the energy required to convert one mole of a substance into gaseous atoms
the energy needed to melt one mole of a solid
the energy released during combustion of one mole of substance
questions.explanation: Enthalpy of atomisation is the energy needed to break all bonds and produce gaseous atoms from one mole of an element or compound; it is always positive.

questions.q: For the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas between the same initial and final volumes, the magnitude of work done by the gas is
options: greater in the reversible process than in a single-step irreversible process
exactly the same in both processes
questions.explanation: A reversible process proceeds through a continuous series of near-equilibrium states, extracting the maximum possible work; any irreversible path against a smaller effective pressure does less work for the same volume change.

questions.q: Resonance energy of a molecule is the energy difference between the actual (hybrid) structure and
questions.explanation: Resonance energy is defined relative to the most stable single (canonical) Lewis structure; the true molecule is more stable (lower energy) than this by the resonance energy.

questions.q: The maximum useful (non-expansion) work obtainable from a spontaneous process at constant temperature and pressure is
options: zero, since all such work becomes heat
questions.explanation: At constant $T,P$, the decrease in Gibbs energy ($-\Delta G$) equals the maximum work obtainable other than pressure–volume work.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about spontaneity is correct?
options: spontaneity guarantees that a reaction is exothermic
a spontaneous reaction always proceeds instantaneously
a thermodynamically spontaneous reaction (e.g. diamond → graphite, $\Delta G<0$) can still be kinetically very slow
if $\Delta G > 0$, a reaction can still occur rapidly
questions.explanation: Thermodynamic spontaneity ($\Delta G < 0$) only tells us a reaction can occur; the rate depends on kinetics (activation energy), so a spontaneous reaction may proceed extremely slowly.

questions.q: The entropy change for vaporisation of 1 mol of water at its boiling point (373 K, $\Delta_{vap}H = 40.7$ kJ mol$^{-1}$) is

Given $\Delta_cH(C, \text{graphite}) = -393.5$, $\Delta_cH(H_2) = -285.8$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, and $C_2H_6(g) + \tfrac72O_2(g) \to 2CO_2(g) + 3H_2O(l)$, $\Delta H = -1560$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, the enthalpy of formation of C$_2$H$_6$(g) is
A system that can exchange only energy, but not matter, with its surroundings is called a(n)
questions.explanation: A closed system allows energy transfer across its boundary but not matter transfer (e.g. a sealed, conducting container).

questions.q: A gas expands against a constant external pressure of 2 atm from 2 L to 6 L. The work done (w, IUPAC convention) is (1 L atm = 101.3 J)
questions.explanation: $w = -p_{ext}\Delta V = -2\times(6-2) = -8$ L atm $= -8\times101.3 \approx -810$ J.

questions.q: All naturally occurring spontaneous processes are thermodynamically
questions.explanation: A truly reversible process is an idealised, infinitely slow limit; all real (spontaneous) processes occurring at a finite rate are irreversible.

questions.q: For a reaction with $\Delta H \approx 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$ (e.g. mixing of ideal gases), the reaction is
questions.explanation: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S \approx -T\Delta S$, which is negative for any $T > 0$ when $\Delta S > 0$, so the process is spontaneous at all temperatures.

questions.q: For a monoatomic ideal gas, the ratio $C_p/C_v$ ($\gamma$) is approximately
questions.explanation: For a monoatomic gas, $C_v = \tfrac32R$ and $C_p = \tfrac52R$, so $\gamma = C_p/C_v = 5/3 \approx 1.67$.

questions.q: In an exothermic reaction,
options: the enthalpy of products is less than that of reactants
heat is absorbed from the surroundings
the enthalpy of products is greater than that of reactants
questions.explanation: In an exothermic reaction heat is released to the surroundings, so the products end up at a lower enthalpy than the reactants, making $\Delta H = H_{products} - H_{reactants}$ negative.
